text: Baselines told us what a forecast costs when we try nothing clever. Exponential smoothing and ARIMA are the two classic statistical families that try to do better, still industry workhorses because they're fast, need no feature engineering, and give honest uncertainty ranges. We fit both on the same sales series and compare them to the seasonal naive baseline.

Exponential smoothing is a weighted average of the past where recent points count more. Simple exponential smoothing tracks only a level. Holt's method adds a trend. Holt-Winters adds a seasonal pattern on top. On our data, the fitted alpha came out to one point zero, meaning S.E.S. collapses into the naive forecast -- M.A.E. of seventeen point seven five, identical to Lesson 8.

Holt lands on the drift baseline's sixteen point six three. Only when we tell Holt-Winters about the weekly cycle, with seasonal_periods equals seven, does the error actually drop -- to six point eight six, against sixteen point one three for seasonal naive. The lesson: these models need the seasonality stated explicitly, or they can lose to a baseline.

A.R.I.M.A. of p, d, q combines three parts: A.R. of p regresses on the series' own last p values, I of d differences it d times to remove trend, and M.A. of q regresses on the last q forecast errors. A plain ARIMA one-one-one scored twenty-two point seven, worse than every baseline, because it knows nothing about the weekly cycle.

Adding a seasonal order of zero-one-one-seven cut that to ten point nine one, and two extra non-seasonal terms brought the best model, ARIMA two-one-two with that seasonal order, down to six point seven two. We choose the order by A.I.C. on training data, not by peeking at test-set error, which would quietly leak the test set.

Statistical models give a range, not just a line. The ninety-five percent forecast interval from our best SARIMA model covered ninety-six percent of the twenty-eight actual values -- close to what a well-calibrated interval should do -- and it widens as the horizon grows, since uncertainty accumulates.

Exponential smoothing builds up level, then trend, then season. ARIMA is autoregression, differencing, and moving-average errors, with a seasonal order doing the same for the season. Both need seasonality stated explicitly. One twenty-eight day window is a single test -- confirm with a backtest before you trust it. Next: Prophet, built to make this workflow easier.
